title: How We Accidentally Invented Government
subtitle: Nobody sat down and designed the state. It grew out of grain, walls, and the need to manage more people than anyone could know.
hook: For most of history, humans lived in groups small enough that everyone knew everyone — no police, no taxes, no bureaucrats. Then cities happened, and suddenly thousands of strangers had to coexist, defend stored grain, and settle disputes. Out of that mess, almost by accident, came the **state**: rulers, taxes, records, and rules enforced on people you'll never meet. Today: how large-scale cooperation got engineered.

sections.heading: The problem cities created
sections.body:
Surplus and trade (our last two History lessons) pulled people into cities. But a city of strangers has problems a village never did: Who protects the granary? Who settles a dispute between people with no shared kin? Who organizes the irrigation everyone depends on? 

A chief who knows everyone can't scale to thousands. So societies grew **impersonal machinery**: written laws, appointed officials, standing guards, and taxes to pay for it all. The state is what you build when cooperation has to work between people who don't trust each other personally.

sections.caption: Cities of strangers created needs that personal ties couldn't meet — so impersonal institutions (law, taxes, bureaucracy) filled the gap.

sections.label: Bureaucracy was a technology
sections.body: We roll our eyes at bureaucracy, but appointed officials keeping written records was a genuine breakthrough — it let a ruler govern people and places far beyond personal reach. Egypt's scribes, China's mandarins, Rome's administrators: the same invention, letting authority scale from a village to an empire. Bureaucracy is how a state remembers and acts at distance.

sections.label: The bargain
sections.body: States offered a deal: give up some freedom and pay taxes, get security and order in return. It's a bargain humans have renegotiated ever since — every debate about the size of government is an argument over the terms of that ancient trade.

sections.caption: How the first cities and states rose in Mesopotamia and beyond.

takeaways: Cities of **strangers** created needs (defense, disputes, shared infrastructure) villages never had.
Personal, know-everyone rule can't scale — so societies built **impersonal institutions**.
The **state** = written law + taxes + bureaucracy enforced on people you'll never meet.
**Bureaucracy** was a real technology: it let authority scale from village to empire.
The state's core bargain — freedom & taxes for security & order — is still being renegotiated today.

quiz.q: Why couldn't 'everyone knows everyone' governance scale to cities?
options: Thousands of strangers need impersonal rules, not personal relationships
quiz.explain: Personal trust doesn't scale; impersonal machinery (law, officials) does.

options: Appointed officials + written records let authority act far beyond personal reach
quiz.explain: Records and officials let a ruler govern people and places they'd never personally see.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: This ties back to the writing lesson. How?
options: Writing (born to track surplus) is exactly what made law, taxes, and bureaucracy possible
quiz.explain: Surplus → writing to track it → the record-keeping that lets a state administer strangers. The chain continues.

options: Let strangers cooperate at scale (defense, disputes, infrastructure)
tg_quiz.correct: Right — impersonal machinery for people who can't all know each other.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's about scaling cooperation among strangers — law, taxes, bureaucracy.
tg_quiz.explain: Personal trust doesn't scale to a city; institutions do.
